title: Watch a Band Perform the Sound Effects from Pink Floyd’s “Money,” Using  a Money Counter, Torn Sheets of Paper & More

body:
When Pink Floyd record­ed “Mon­ey” in 1972, Roger Waters spliced into the open­ing moments the sounds of cash reg­is­ters, tear­ing paper, and jin­gling coins. Half a cen­tu­ry lat­er, the Ger­man drum­mer Sina Doer­ing and her band per­formed those sounds live, using a bowl of loose change, a toy reg­is­ter, a mon­ey counter, and a sheet of paper torn on the beat. And they did it all live at Abbey Road Stu­dios, the same place where Pink Floyd record­ed Dark Side of the Moon (on which “Mon­ey” appears). Watch it above, and enjoy.

title: The Native History of NYC's Oysters
description:
Daily Newsletter
                Who needs IMAX? See a real papyrus fragment of Homer’s Odyssey at The Met.
body:
Daily Newsletter
                Who needs IMAX? See a real papyrus fragment of Homer’s Odyssey at The Met.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
        
            The oyster, writes Hrag Vartanian, is "no incidental New Yorker, but perhaps its most symbolic creature." Hyperallergic's co-founder and editor-at-large visits Mohawk artist Alan Michelson’s poetic installation in Governor’s Island, where about a million oyster shells culled from Manhattan restaurants stir reflections on Native land and historical memory. Vartanian muses on the glorious mollusk’s history, from Lenape shell middens to NYC’s menus to the detrimental effects of their disappearance on our ecosystems. In Michelson’s work, Vartanian writes, “the shells become forces of insurgency, counter-experts that quietly refute settler innocence and its alibi that ‘nothing was here’ before extraction.”Still can’t get a ticket for Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey in New York? Welcome to the club. Here’s a cooler plan: Head uptown to The Met to see a rare, 2,300-year-old fragment with lines from Homer’s epic, now on view at the museum. No hot takes about the historical accuracy of Bronze Age armor required. Papyrus > IMAX.—Valentina Di Liscia, senior editor

	
		
			The Lost Pearls of New York City
		
	
	
		Walking down Pearl Street in Manhattan’s Chinatown, you probably don’t realize that the name marks the original 17th-century East River shoreline of New York City. In fact, the street was named for a Lenape shell midden that was located on its southern section, which is also believed to have been adjacent to a Lenape canoe landing. It was one of many prominent middens that marked the region, and as Mark Kurlansky explains in his bestselling book The Big Oyster: History on the Half Shell (2006), middens are “the most common marker of a pre-European settlement anywhere in the area of the mouth of the Hudson.” These piles of oyster shells, he notes, were sometimes as much as four feet deep, sometimes buried in the ground, sometimes piled high. | Hrag Vartanian

title: Joeun Kim Aatchim’s Layered Lines Summon Translucent Worlds
description: In Joeun Kim Aatchim’s paintings—but she calls them drawings—everything is so vivid, yet so elusive. Her line feels definitive, yet the images they
body:
In Joeun Kim Aatchim’s paintings—but she calls them drawings—everything is so vivid, yet so elusive. Her line feels definitive, yet the images they convey seem to fade away into sheer luminosity. 

	Her works are typically painted using mineral pigment in shellac—sometimes with watercolor, pastel, or other materials—on layers of silk that, stretched across frames, show through to the wall behind. They’re all about one image being seen through another—not different things, in the manner of Francis Picabia’s transparencies, but different versions of the same thing; different attempts, a little like the way Henri Matisse would partially overpaint his works to show multiple thoughts about how to depict one thing, or how to position it within the composition. 
	

	
		Related Articles
	


	Aatchim speaks about her method as being a layering of first drafts. “Rather than working on a piece over and over to make it perfect,” she told me, “I can keep my first thought” even as the piece develops. The result is a bouquet of essays, finding resolution in the tentative. She calls what she does “drawing” because she considers it “a thought in progress,” and because her materials never completely cover the surface she’s working on. “It doesn’t matter if it’s pencil or chalk or paint. If it doesn’t cover the surface, I consider that a drawing, whether it’s on the floor, on the street, or on the wall, or an object.”

	The Korean-born artist has been exhibiting widely since earning her MFA at Columbia University in 2017, where she’d gone at the suggestion of Kiki Smith, to whom she’d been an assistant. Since then, she’s had solo shows at galleries in New York, Los Angeles, Guadalajara, Seoul, and Madrid. Coming later this year is her first exhibition in São Paulo, at Almeida & Dale. I caught up with Aatchim not in her Brooklyn studio but in Seoul, by Zoom, while she was visiting her parents. Was she working there? “I tried to rest, but I don’t know how to rest, and I don’t have any hobbies,” she said. “I started thinking, maybe I’m nobody if I’m not making art. So I started making work in the dining room.” In any case, she added, the materials she likes to use are more readily available in Korea than in New York.
	

	But maybe, her real material is mnemonic. She considers her vivid sense of recall to be both a blessing and a curse. She explains that “memories I haven’t drawn yet keep lingering in my head, and have to be stored somewhere. You know, because I stored this somewhere safe, I can now get new memories.” That probably explains why her simple yet multilayered portraits of friends and observations of her everyday world can be at once so clear and distinct yet so intangible. After all, memories can’t be fixed. They’re always thoughts in progress.
